summary: Babel MAC authentication (RFC 8967) checks packet counters to resist replay attacks, but strict checking can drop legitimate packets that arrive out of order. This document relaxes the verification rules so the protocol copes better with packet reordering. It updates RFC 8967.

eli5.summary: If numbered letters sometimes arrive in the wrong order, a strict clerk throws away good ones. This lets the clerk be a bit more forgiving, while still catching copies.

questions: why does babel drop multicast packets on wifi

subtitle: Two ways to stop Babel's replay protection from dropping good packets that merely arrive out of order.

tldr.problem: Babel MAC authentication (RFC 8967) drops any packet whose Packet Counter is not higher than the last one seen, which fails on some wireless links where multicast packets are delayed behind unicast ones.
tldr.mechanism: Keep separate highest Packet Counter values for unicast and multicast packets, and optionally keep a window of recently seen counter values so a bounded amount of reordering is tolerated.
tldr.outcome: Replay protection is kept, since the destination address is covered by the MAC. This RFC updates RFC 8967 and recommends the split-state method, while the window is optional.

today: RFC 9467 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8967 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Strict Counter Checking Breaks
sections.content:
The Babel MAC authentication mechanism in RFC 8967 assumes packet reordering is exceptional and drops any packet that arrives out of order. That is generally true on wired links but not on some wireless ones.

IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) defines power-saving modes that let stations switch their radio off for extended periods, in the hundreds of milliseconds. The access point buffers all multicast packets and sends them after the interval ends. Multicast packets are therefore delayed by up to a few hundred milliseconds relative to unicast packets, which under some traffic patterns makes the Packet Counter (PC) check systematically fail for multicast packets.

The document gives two relaxations. Using separate unicast and multicast state is RECOMMENDED, the window is OPTIONAL, and the two MAY be combined. It does not change the protocol's security properties.
sections.eli5: A school bus sometimes holds back the group announcements while the personal notes go straight through. The announcements arrive late, and a strict rule wrongly says they are old.

sections.title: How the Packet Counter Works Today
sections.content:
Babel MAC authentication prevents replay by putting a strictly increasing Packet Counter (PC) on every sent packet. Despite the name, it does not truly count packets: a sender may increase it by more than one between two packets.

A receiver remembers the highest PC from each neighbour. A new packet whose PC is smaller or equal is discarded. Otherwise it is accepted and the highest value is updated.

There is no one-to-one match between sender state and receiver states. Several receivers track one sender, and they are not necessarily identical, because unicast packets and packets received by only a subset of receivers update only some of them.
sections.eli5: Each letter has a bigger number than the last. The receiver remembers the biggest number seen and rejects anything that is not bigger.

sections.title: Separate Unicast and Multicast Counters
sections.content:
Instead of one highest PC per neighbour, the receiver keeps two: the highest multicast value PCm and the highest unicast value PCu. The neighbour table entry becomes the triple (Index, PCm, PCu), where Index is an arbitrary string of 0 to 32 octets and each PC is a 32-bit integer.

A successful Challenge Reply stores the Index and sets both PCm and PCu to the PC in the TLV. For other packets, the receiver compares the PC to PCm if the packet went to a multicast address, or to PCu otherwise. If the PC is smaller or equal the packet MUST be dropped, with no challenge sent because the mismatch may be harmless reordering. Otherwise that same field is updated and the packet is accepted. The RFC gives OLD and NEW replacement text for the two affected bullets in Section 4.3 of RFC 8967.

The RFC warns against generalising this to more counters, for example per TOS value or per 802.11 access category. Choosing a counter by a field the MAC does not protect would let an attacker replay a packet by changing that field.
sections.eli5: Instead of one pile of tickets, there are two piles: one for group announcements and one for personal notes. Each pile has its own rule, so a late announcement is not judged against personal notes.

sections.title: Window-Based Verification
sections.content:
This method is similar to Section 3.4.3 of RFC 4303. Besides the highest PC PCh, the receiver keeps a window of booleans, size S, covering PC values just below PCh. The default S=128 is RECOMMENDED. The entry becomes (Index, PCh, Window).

For each packet the receiver computes the index i = PC - PCh + S - 1 and then:

  1. If i is negative, the packet is too old and MUST be discarded.
  2. If i is below S, check the window slot. If already set, the PC was seen before and the packet MUST be discarded. Otherwise mark it and accept.
  3. If i is at least S, the window MUST be shifted left by PC - PCh, PCh is set to the PC, the rightmost slot is set, and the packet is accepted.

On a successful Challenge Reply, PCh is set to the received value and all window slots are reset except the one at index S - 1, which is set.
sections.eli5: The clerk keeps a checklist of the last 128 ticket numbers. A late ticket is fine if its box is not yet ticked. A ticket that is too old, or already ticked, is thrown out.

sections.title: Combining Both Techniques
sections.content:
The two techniques are complementary. Splitting state lets multicast be reordered against unicast by any number of PC values, while the window lets any packets be reordered by a bounded number.

An implementation using both MUST keep two windows per neighbour table entry, one for multicast and one for unicast. A successful Challenge Reply resets both. Other packets are checked against the multicast window if the destination is a multicast address and against the unicast window otherwise.
sections.eli5: You can use both ideas: two checklists, one for announcements and one for personal notes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures do not change the security properties in Section 1.2 of RFC 8967. Choosing between the multicast and unicast counter uses the packet's destination IP address, which is in the pseudo-header and so is covered by the MAC. An attacker cannot change it without breaking the MAC, so a unicast packet cannot be replayed as multicast or the reverse.

The extra per-neighbour state is marginal, between 4 and 36 octets depending on implementation choices, and should not significantly affect resistance to denial-of-service attacks. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The address on the envelope is stamped with the secret seal, so nobody can move a letter from one pile to the other without being noticed.
